text: I’ll model the wing with span along \(y\), freestream along \(+x\), and the NACA section in \(x\)-\(z\) planes. The unswept leading edge stays at \(x=0\); the root is attached to the domain plane \(y=0\). I’ll interpret the requested clearances as 3 root chords beyond the tip and 3 root chords above and below the section, with inlet/outlet measured from the root leading/trailing edges. I’ll use a Cartesian background mesh and snappyHexMesh for the external air volume. First I’m creating the lofted solid at coarse profile resolution and rendering it with the proposed domain.

The first view exposed an ambiguity in “to each side and above.” For a wall-mounted half-wing, the physically consistent interpretation is a horizontal root wall, span in \(+z\), and lateral clearances on both \(y\) sides. I’m adopting that orientation: \(z=0\) is the root wall, the tip is at \(z=0.2\) m, lateral bounds are \(y=\pm0.36\) m, and the top is \(z=0.56\) m. I’ll now generate the five explicitly named STL patch files; the wing STL contains the exposed loft and tip only, not the buried root cap.

The geometry view now confirms the intended wall-mounted orientation and clearances. The NACA formula produces a tiny numerical leading-edge \(x\) overshoot of \(4\,\mu\text{m}\), negligible relative to the 120 mm chord and retained rather than clipping the specified profile. I’ll create a coarse background mesh of about 10,000 cells, with the five boundary names already assigned on the block and the wing ready for local castellated refinement.

The background mesh is exactly 0.04 m isotropic, 9,828 cells, and its measured bounds match the requested/assumed domain extents. I’ll now cut out the wing solid and snap the surrounding air mesh to the exposed wing STL, refining the wing surface to roughly 5–10 mm for this coarse pass.

snappyHexMesh stopped before modifying the mesh because OpenFOAM 2512 requires minimal finite-volume dictionaries even for meshing. I’ll add only those required empty/default dictionaries and rerun; no solver setup or boundary conditions are being introduced.

The external mesh completed with 16,873 cells and no snappy quality errors. I’ll now run the binding topology/geometry checks and inspect patch sizes, especially the wing–root-wall junction, before deciding whether the coarse mesh is acceptable.

The exhaustive check confirms one connected external-air region, all five patches, closed overall boundary, positive volumes, max non-orthogonality \(54.9^\circ\), and max skewness 1.81. Its optional plane-based diagnostic flags 736 concave cut cells near the thin airfoil; I’ll inspect the actual mesh cross-section and also run standard checkMesh, which is the binding OpenFOAM acceptance test.

Standard checkMesh reports **Mesh OK**. I’ll render a horizontal section at mid-span and the wing boundary itself to verify that the air cells surround—rather than fill—the NACA profile and that the taper is visible in the final mesh.

The preview confirms an open airfoil-shaped hole in the mid-span air mesh and a continuous tapered wing patch. I’ll repeat the visualization cell with an explicit display import so the retained `build.py` remains reproducible outside the notebook kernel.
I’ll make the preview-display cell fully self-contained by importing both required names.

To make the exported patch set geometrically watertight as a union—not merely watertight after meshing—I’ll replace the two-triangle root-wall STL with a triangulated rectangle containing an exact NACA-root opening. Its opening vertices will match the exposed wing skin’s root edge, while it remains a single `rootWall.stl` patch.

The exact-match check found the root opening vertices coincide, but Gmsh also revealed that my closed profile list retained a duplicate trailing-edge endpoint. Although the mesh passed, that creates zero-area STL facets. I’ll correct the tessellation by storing each closed-loop vertex once, regenerate the wing and holed root-wall STLs, and then remesh from the background block.

The repaired wing STL has 600 nondegenerate facets; the smallest area is \(3.89\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{m^2}\), with zero zero-area facets. I’ll rebuild and recheck the mesh against this corrected surface.

The rebuilt mesh again passes standard checkMesh with unchanged quality and one connected region. I’ll now validate the five STL files as one welded surface, checking free edges, multiply-used edges, orientation consistency, and self-intersections; the temporary combined diagnostic STL will be removed afterward so `constant/triSurface` retains exactly one file per patch.

The union diagnostic correctly caught two export issues not visible to snappy: Gmsh subdivided the root-wall rectangle’s outer edges, creating T-junctions against the four coarse domain patches, and the wing normals were oriented out of the solid rather than out of the **air** volume. I’ll preserve the profile-hole refinement but force each outer root-wall edge to remain one segment, reverse the wing STL winding for the external-fluid convention, and rerun the union test.
The root patch now uses only the four requested domain corners on its outer perimeter while retaining all 200 airfoil-hole vertices. I’ll repeat the welded-union checks.

The corrected five-file STL union is closed, has one connected part, one consistent-normal zone, no illegal triangles, and no self-intersections. I’ll perform one final mesh rebuild using exactly these final STL files, then report measured planform/profile invariants and the final checkMesh statistics.
